title: Organismal Biology — Plant & Animal Organ Systems

days.title: Introduction to Organ Systems and Their Functions
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Identify the major organ systems in plants and animals.
  • Describe the primary function of each organ system.
  • Compare how plants and animals perform similar life processes.
  • Recognize that organ systems work together to maintain life.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Organ System — a group of organs that work together to perform a specific function.
  • Organismal Biology — the study of structure, function, and behavior of whole organisms.
  • Homeostasis — maintenance of a stable internal environment.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Why Organ Systems Matter

Every living organism must perform the same fundamental life processes — but plants and animals do them in very different ways.

B. The Nine Life Processes We Compare

#ProcessAnimalsPlants
1ReproductionSexual & asexualSexual & asexual
2DevelopmentEmbryo → adultSeed → mature plant
3NutritionHeterotrophicAutotrophic
4Gas ExchangeLungs, gillsStomata, lenticels
5TransportHeart, blood vesselsXylem, phloem
6Body FluidsKidneysVacuoles, stomata
7ControlNervous, endocrineHormones
8ImmuneWBCs, antibodiesBarriers, chemicals
9Sensory/MotorEyes, musclesTropisms

C. Major Animal Organ Systems

SystemOrgansFunction
CirculatoryHeart, vessels, bloodTransport
RespiratoryLungs, trachea, gillsGas exchange
DigestiveMouth, stomach, intestinesBreakdown & absorb food
NervousBrain, spinal cord, nervesDetect & respond
EndocrineGlandsHormones
ExcretoryKidneys, bladderRemove wastes
Immune/LymphaticLymph nodes, WBCsDefense
ReproductiveGonadsOffspring
Muscular/SkeletalMuscles, bonesSupport, movement

D. Major Plant Organ Systems

SystemStructuresFunction
Shoot SystemLeaves, stems, flowersPhotosynthesis, reproduction
Root SystemRoots, root hairsAnchor, absorb water/minerals
Vascular SystemXylem, phloemTransport water, nutrients, sugars
Dermal SystemEpidermis, cuticleProtection, gas exchange

E. Comparative Preview

Today we set the stage. Over the next three days, we'll go deeper into how these systems work and how they maintain homeostasis — the body's internal balance.

💬 Let's Discuss

A single cell can do everything itself. A large organism cannot: a cell deep inside your body is too far from the outside world to get its own food and oxygen or get rid of its own wastes. The solution is division of labor. Cells form tissues, tissues form organs, and organs work together as organ systems, each specializing in one life process while depending on the others.

Animals and plants face the same basic problems — getting nutrients, exchanging gases, moving materials, removing wastes, responding to the environment and reproducing — but solve them differently because of how they live. Animals move to find food (heterotrophs), so they have digestive, muscular and fast nervous systems. Plants stay in one place and make their own food (autotrophs), so they rely on two big systems: the shoot system (stems, leaves, flowers) above ground and the root system below, connected by vascular tissue — xylem and phloem.

Compare matching jobs: animals exchange gases in lungs or gills, plants through stomata; animals pump blood with a heart, plants move water using transpiration pull in the xylem; animals filter wastes in kidneys, plants store some wastes in vacuoles or drop them with old leaves. Some processes are shared by both — every living cell carries out cellular respiration.

Systems also cooperate. During a run, the respiratory system takes in O₂, the circulatory system delivers it, muscles use it, and the nervous system coordinates everything.

Common mistake: thinking plants "breathe in CO₂ instead of O₂." Plants take in CO₂ for photosynthesis, but they also take in O₂ for respiration, day and night.

pairs.why: The circulatory system transports nutrients, gases and wastes.

pairs.right: Gas exchange — O₂ in, CO₂ out
pairs.why: The respiratory system exchanges O₂ and CO₂.
The digestive system breaks food into absorbable nutrients.
The nervous system detects stimuli and coordinates fast responses.
The endocrine system secretes hormones into the blood.
The excretory system removes wastes and balances fluids.
The immune/lymphatic system defends against pathogens.
Muscles and bones provide support and movement.

scenarios.explanation: Photosynthesis happens in plants (autotrophs).

questions.text: Name three organ systems found in animals but NOT in plants.

choices.label: Root system, stem system, leaf system

questions.explanation: Circulatory, respiratory and nervous systems are animal systems; the rest are plant structures.

questions.text: What structure in plants performs gas exchange?
questions.explanation: Stomata let gases enter and leave the leaf.

questions.text: Why do organisms need organ systems at all?

choices.label: To make the body look more complex
To divide labor among specialized parts
To fill up empty space inside the body
To replace the cells that die every day

questions.explanation: Organ systems divide labor so each life process is done efficiently.

takeaways: Plants and animals perform the same basic life processes with different structures.
Animals rely on organ systems (circulatory, respiratory, nervous, etc.).
Plants rely on shoot and root systems, plus vascular tissues.
All systems work together to maintain homeostasis.

days.title: Animal Organ Systems — Detailed
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Describe the major animal organ systems and their functions.
  • Explain how animal systems work together to maintain life.
  • Identify key organs of each system.
  • Explain how structure enables function in each system.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Organ — a group of tissues that work together for a specific function.
  • System integration — organ systems coordinate for survival.
  • Surface-area-to-volume ratio — drives specialization in exchange surfaces.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Digestive System

  • Function: Break down food into absorbable nutrients
  • Organs: Mouth, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, liver, pancreas
  • Key adaptations: Villi and microvilli increase surface area

B. Circulatory System

  • Function: Transport nutrients, gases, hormones, wastes
  • Organs: Heart, blood vessels, blood
  • Types: Open vs closed

C. Respiratory System

  • Function: Exchange O₂ and CO₂
  • Organs: Lungs, trachea, bronchi, alveoli; gills in fish

D. Nervous System

  • Function: Detect stimuli and coordinate rapid responses
  • Organs: Brain, spinal cord, nerves

E. Endocrine System

  • Function: Secrete hormones for slower, longer-lasting regulation
  • Glands: Hypothalamus, pituitary, thyroid, adrenal, pancreas, gonads

F. Excretory System

  • Function: Remove metabolic wastes, regulate water/salt
  • Organs: Kidneys, ureters, bladder, urethra

G. Immune/Lymphatic System

  • Function: Defend against pathogens
  • Organs: Lymph nodes, spleen, thymus, tonsils, WBCs

H. Reproductive System

  • Function: Produce gametes for species survival
  • Organs: Gonads, ducts, accessory glands

I. Muscular & Skeletal Systems

  • Function: Support, movement, protection
  • Organs: Bones, cartilage, muscles, tendons, ligaments

💬 Let's Discuss

Let us follow one meal through the human body to see how animal organ systems connect. When you eat sinangag and egg, the digestive system breaks starch and protein into glucose and amino acids. Most absorption happens in the small intestine, whose lining is folded into millions of villi, each covered in microvilli — together giving a surface area about the size of a badminton court.

The nutrients enter the circulatory system. The heart, a four-chambered pump, sends blood through arteries, capillaries and veins to every cell. Cells use the glucose in respiration, which needs O₂ — supplied by the respiratory system. Air travels down to about 300 million alveoli, thin-walled air sacs surrounded by capillaries where O₂ diffuses into the blood and CO₂ diffuses out.

Rising blood sugar is detected by the pancreas, part of the endocrine system, which secretes insulin to help cells take up glucose; between meals it releases glucagon. Hormones act slowly but for a long time. The nervous system, with neurons carrying electrical signals, acts in milliseconds — like the reflex that pulls your hand from a hot pan.

Wastes such as urea are removed by the excretory system: each kidney has about a million nephrons that filter blood, reabsorb what is useful, secrete extra wastes and finally excrete urine. Meanwhile, the immune system (lymph nodes, white blood cells) guards against pathogens, and bones and muscles support and move the body.

Common mistake: mixing up villi (intestine, absorption) with alveoli (lungs, gas exchange).

pairs.why: Villi in the small intestine increase surface area for absorbing nutrients.
The heart pumps blood throughout the body.
Alveoli are thin air sacs where O₂ and CO₂ are exchanged.
Neurons carry electrical impulses.
The pancreas releases insulin and glucagon to control blood glucose.
Kidneys filter blood and produce urine.
Lymph nodes filter lymph and house white blood cells.
Bones support the body and protect organs such as the brain and heart.

scenarios.explanation: Blood delivering O₂ to muscles is the circulatory system.

questions.text: Which structure increases surface area for nutrient absorption in the small intestine?
questions.explanation: Villi increase the surface area of the small intestine.

questions.text: Which system releases hormones to regulate body functions over long periods?
questions.explanation: The endocrine system uses hormones for long-term control.

questions.text: Which of the following correctly describes the excretory process?
questions.explanation: Urine forms by filtration, then reabsorption, then secretion, then excretion.

takeaways: Each animal organ system has specialized organs for its function.
Structures are adapted to maximize efficiency (e.g., alveoli, villi).

days.title: Plant Organ Systems — Detailed
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Describe the shoot and root systems in plants.
  • Explain how xylem and phloem transport materials.
  • Describe the dermal system and its protective role.
  • Compare plant structural adaptations to those of animals.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Shoot system — above-ground organs.
  • Root system — below-ground organs.
  • Vascular tissue — xylem (water) and phloem (sugars).
  • Dermal tissue — outer protective layer.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Shoot System

OrganFunctionAdaptations
LeavesPhotosynthesis, gas exchangeBroad surface; stomata; cuticle
StemsSupport, transportVascular bundles
FlowersReproductionAttract pollinators

B. Root System

  • Taproot: One main root (e.g., carrots)
  • Fibrous roots: Many thin roots (e.g., grasses)
  • Root hairs: Increase surface area for absorption

C. Vascular Tissue — Xylem & Phloem

TissueTransportsDirection
XylemWater and mineralsRoots → shoots
PhloemSugars and nutrientsBoth directions

D. Dermal Tissue

  • Epidermis: Outer layer
  • Cuticle: Waxy layer reducing water loss
  • Stomata: Pores for gas exchange

E. Plant vs Animal Adaptations

FunctionPlantsAnimals
Gas exchangeStomataLungs/gills
TransportXylem & phloemHeart & vessels
SupportCell walls, turgorSkeletal system

💬 Let's Discuss

A plant has two connected systems. The shoot system — stems, leaves and flowers — is above ground. Leaves are flat and thin to capture light and exchange gases. Stems hold leaves up toward light and carry materials between roots and leaves. Flowers are the reproductive organs. The root system anchors the plant, absorbs water and minerals, and often stores food. A taproot has one thick main root (carrot, radish, labanos) that reaches deep water and stores starch. Fibrous roots are many thin roots (rice, grasses, corn) that hold soil well — useful against erosion. Tiny root hairs greatly increase the absorbing surface.

The two systems are linked by vascular tissue. Xylem carries water and minerals upward from roots to leaves. There is no pump: as water evaporates from leaves (transpiration), it pulls the next water molecules up, like sipping through a straw. Phloem carries sugars from where they are made or stored (sources, such as leaves) to where they are needed (sinks, such as roots, fruits and growing tips) — so it can flow up or down.

Leaves must balance two needs: letting CO₂ in and keeping water from escaping. A waxy cuticle reduces water loss, while stomata, each controlled by two guard cells, open to let CO₂ in and O₂ and water vapor out. On a hot, dry afternoon, stomata close to save water — even though this slows photosynthesis.

Common mistake: "phloem carries food down only." Phloem moves sugars wherever they are needed, including up to new leaves and fruits.

pairs.why: Leaves are the main site of photosynthesis and gas exchange.
Stems support the plant and carry materials between roots and shoots.
Flowers contain the plant's reproductive organs.
A taproot has one main thick root, as in carrots.
Fibrous roots are many thin roots of similar size, as in grasses.
Xylem moves water and minerals up from the roots.
Phloem moves sugars from sources to sinks in either direction.
Stomata are pores that let gases in and out.

scenarios.explanation: A thick storage root is a taproot.

questions.text: Which tissue transports water and minerals upward in plants?
questions.explanation: Xylem carries water and minerals upward.

questions.explanation: Stomata allow gas exchange and control water loss.

questions.explanation: Root hairs increase the surface area for absorbing water.

takeaways: Plants have shoot and root systems.
Xylem transports water up; phloem transports sugars both ways.
The dermal system protects and controls gas exchange.

days.title: Comparative Processes — Reproduction, Nutrition, Gas Exchange
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Compare reproduction strategies in plants and animals.
  • Compare nutrition modes in plants and animals.
  • Compare gas exchange mechanisms.
  • Explain how each adaptation supports survival.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Sexual vs asexual reproduction — genetic variation vs rapid multiplication.
  • Autotroph vs heterotroph — make own food vs consume others.
  • Diffusion surface — thin, moist, large surface for gas exchange.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Reproduction

AspectAnimalsPlants
SexualGametes → zygotePollination → seed
AsexualBudding, fragmentationRunners, tubers, bulbs
Advantage of sexualGenetic diversity → adaptation
Advantage of asexualFast, no mate required

B. Nutrition

AspectAnimalsPlants
ModeHeterotrophicAutotrophic
Source of carbonOrganic foodCO₂ from air
Energy sourceChemical energyLight energy
Key structuresMouth, digestive systemLeaves, chloroplasts, roots

C. Gas Exchange

AspectAnimalsPlants
OrgansLungs, gills, skinStomata, lenticels
O₂ intakeActive (breathing)Passive (diffusion)
CO₂ releaseExhaleDiffuse through stomata

D. Why These Differences?

  • Animals are motile → need active systems.
  • Plants are sessile → rely on diffusion and environment.
  • Each group's structures reflect its environmental niche.

💬 Let's Discuss

Plants and animals solve the same three problems — getting nutrients, exchanging gases and reproducing — in different but comparable ways. Comparing them helps you remember both.

Nutrition. Plants are autotrophs: they make their own sugar by photosynthesis and absorb minerals from soil through roots. Animals are heterotrophs: they ingest other organisms and digest them into small molecules that can be absorbed. Both then use those molecules for energy and growth.

Gas exchange. Both rely on diffusion across moist, thin surfaces. Animals usually ventilate actively: fish push water over gills; mammals breathe air into lungs, where alveoli give a huge surface. Blood with hemoglobin then carries O₂. Plants have no breathing movements; gases diffuse through stomata into air spaces inside the leaf, and no special carrier is needed.

Reproduction. Both can reproduce sexually, combining gametes to create genetic diversity. In flowering plants, pollination transfers pollen to the stigma, followed by fertilization and the formation of seeds and fruit. In mammals, internal fertilization is followed by development in the uterus, where the placenta nourishes the embryo. Both can also reproduce asexually: plants by runners, cuttings or tubers (sweet potato, banana suckers), and some animals by budding (hydra) or fragmentation (starfish). Asexual reproduction is fast but produces identical offspring.

Common mistake: "Only plants reproduce asexually." Many animals do too, and most plants also reproduce sexually through flowers.

pairs.why: Pollination moves pollen to the stigma so fertilization can occur in plants.
The placenta connects mother and embryo in mammals to supply nutrients.
Photosynthesis is how plants make their own food from sunlight.
Digestion breaks food down so animals can absorb nutrients.
Plants exchange gases through stomata.
Animals exchange gases in alveoli of the lungs.

scenarios.text: Produces seeds after pollination.
scenarios.explanation: Seeds form after pollination in flowering plants.

scenarios.text: Uses hemoglobin to carry oxygen in blood.
scenarios.explanation: Hemoglobin in blood is an animal feature.

scenarios.text: Absorbs CO₂ through stomata.
scenarios.explanation: CO₂ enters plants through stomata.

scenarios.text: Uses gills or lungs for gas exchange.
scenarios.explanation: Gills and lungs are animal gas-exchange organs.

scenarios.text: Has an autotrophic mode of nutrition.
scenarios.explanation: Autotrophic nutrition (making food) is a plant feature.

scenarios.text: Can reproduce asexually.
scenarios.explanation: Both plants (cuttings, runners) and animals (budding) can reproduce asexually.

questions.text: Which statement correctly compares nutrition in plants and animals?

choices.label: Plants are autotrophic; animals are heterotrophic
Plants are heterotrophic; animals are autotrophic

questions.explanation: Plants make their own food (autotrophs); animals must eat (heterotrophs).

questions.text: How does gas exchange differ between plants and animals?

choices.label: Both breathe actively using lungs or gills
Animals ventilate lungs or gills; plants use stomata
Plants use lungs and animals use stomata
Neither needs gas exchange to stay alive

questions.explanation: Animals breathe actively with lungs or gills; plants rely on passive diffusion through stomata.

questions.text: Which mode of reproduction provides genetic diversity in both plants and animals?
questions.explanation: Sexual reproduction combines genes from two parents, giving diversity.

takeaways: Plants and animals perform the same life processes but with different structures.
Animals use active systems; plants rely on diffusion.
Reproduction can be sexual or asexual in both groups.
Nutrition: animals are heterotrophs; most plants are autotrophs.
